title: The same event, recorded twice
task: Say what the difference between the two records means.
scene: Inês Cardoso has two records of the same earthquake, from stations eleven hundred metres apart. One trace is short and sharp. The other is three times taller and runs half a minute longer.
assumes: an instrument records the shaking where it stands, not the earthquake itself
takeaway: A record describes one place, so two records of one earthquake can disagree and both be right.
question: What does the difference between the two records mean?
why: The earthquake was one event. What each instrument recorded is what its own ground did. The bench is granite, and granite passes shaking on nearly unchanged. The Flats are soft fill, and soft ground shakes harder and for longer. Here the soft site moved about three times as far as the rock site. That is the ground, not a bigger earthquake under one town. It is also why one number for a whole town is a poor number.
answerText: The Flats record is about three times the rock one, because the ground there is soft fill. Same earthquake, different ground underneath.

choices: One of the two instruments is faulty, and its record should be thrown out.
The soft ground under the Flats shook harder, and for longer.
The Flats are closer to where it started, so the shaking there was stronger.
The Flats record has aftershocks in it that the other station missed.
rebuttals: Both instruments checked out against a third sensor this morning. The difference is real.
Eleven hundred metres is nothing against a source twenty kilometres away. Distance cannot make it three times bigger.
Both records cover the same ninety seconds, and the aftershocks are on separate traces.

title: Ground that people put there
task: Match each kind of ground to what it does when it is shaken.
scene: Navarro has an 1892 survey and a photograph from 1948. Where Bay Road runs now there was a tidal creek. The port was pumped into place out of a dredger over four summers.
assumes: ground can be natural, or it can be put there by people
saturated means every gap between the grains is already full of water
takeaway: Loose, wet, young ground behaves in a way old rock does not.
why: Fill that is pumped in through water lands loose, and it stays full of water. Shake it and the grains try to shuffle closer together. The water in the gaps cannot get out fast enough, so the water takes the load instead of the grains. Grains that are not pressing on each other cannot hold anything up, and the ground behaves like a thick liquid. Old ground has had a hundred centuries to pack down. This has had eighty years.

scenarios: Fill pumped in from a dredger in the 1940s.
The granite bench under Upper Town.
The line of the old tidal creek.
Ground that has sat in place for ten thousand years.
choices: Loose and full of water, so shaking packs it down and squeezes the water.
Stiff and dry, so it passes the shaking on almost unchanged.
The loosest and wettest of the lot, which is where the sand came up.
Squeezed tight by its own weight over time, which is why age helps.
rebuttals: Fill dropped through water settles loose and stays wet. That is what pumping it in does to it.
The granite bench is neither loose nor wet, so shaking does something else entirely to it.
The old creek line holds the loosest, wettest material, which is why the sand fans follow it.
Age matters because ground packs down over time, and eighty years is young.
columns: What it does when it is shaken

title: Where the first day of assessment goes
task: Spend the six assessor-days, then see which questions the plan can still answer.
scene: Six assessors are free for one day. Four hundred families are waiting on a decision in the Flats. Marina Court and the Parade are already fenced off, and Upper Town is mostly lived in.
assumes: an inspection queue is a decision, not a list
takeaway: Spend a team on the questions whose answers can still change what happens today.
question: Can your plan still get the waiting Flats families a decision today, knowing some questions have to wait?
why: There are six assessor-days and more good work than that. Every inspection bought is another one given up. The Flats sweep can send four hundred families home tonight, or keep them out on purpose. Marina Court and the Parade have fences doing that job already, so more detail there changes little today. Upper Town is useful and not urgent. Buy the answer that can still change what happens.
answerText: Keep at least four assessor-days on the Flats, so the waiting families get a decision today. Spend what is left on one more question. The team cannot buy all four, and the rest wait.

title: How far away it started
task: Turn the gap between the two arrivals into a distance.
scene: The vault trace shows the first wave at 04:12:19 and the strong shaking at 04:12:32. Cardoso wants a distance before anybody draws a circle on a map.
assumes: the first wave travels faster than the strong shaking that follows it
takeaway: The gap between the two arrivals grows with distance, so one station gives a distance and three give a place.
question: How far away did it start?
why: Both waves leave at the same moment, and one of them travels faster. So the gap between them grows the further you are from the source. Close in they arrive almost together. A hundred kilometres away there are thirteen seconds between them. That gap gives a distance, and a distance on its own is a circle round the station. Three stations give three circles, and where they cross is where it started.
answerText: About a hundred kilometres away. That is a circle drawn round this station, not a spot on the map.

estimate.prompt: The first wave arrived at nineteen seconds past, and the strong shaking at thirty-two. Count about eight kilometres for each second between them.
estimate.question: How far away did it start?
estimate.relationship: Distance = the gap in seconds × eight kilometres.
estimate.explanation: The magnitude and the depth are both real numbers about this earthquake, and neither belongs here. One is how big it was. One is how deep. This is how far.
estimate.solution: Thirty-two take away nineteen is thirteen seconds. Thirteen times eight is a hundred and four kilometres.
givens: The gap between the two arrivals is thirteen seconds
Count about eight kilometres for each second of that gap
labels: 32 s (strong shaking, seconds past the minute)
19 s (first wave, seconds past the minute)
8 km for each second of the gap

title: Why the number moved
task: Explain what changed between the two magnitudes.
scene: Tanaka has both bulletins on the desk. The early one used the first stations to report. The later one used the whole network, hours afterwards.
assumes: a magnitude is worked out from records, so more records can change it
takeaway: A number that changes means the measurement improved. The event did not change.
question: Which explanation of the change from 6.6 to 6.8 holds up?
why: A magnitude is not read off the ground. It is worked out from what the instruments recorded, so it gets better as more of them report. The first bulletin used the handful of stations that had answered in the first minutes. The later one used the whole network. Going from 6.6 to 6.8 sounds tiny, and it is not. That step means about twice the energy. The earthquake never changed. How much of it had been measured did.
answerText: The later figure used more stations, and more of each record. A step of 0.2 is about twice the energy. It is a better measurement, not a bigger earthquake.

choices: The earthquake got stronger during the six hours between the bulletins.
The later figure used more stations, and more of each record.
One agency made a mistake, and it should be corrected in public.
The two figures are on different scales and cannot be compared at all.
rebuttals: The earthquake was over in under a minute. Nothing about it changed six hours later.
Neither agency was wrong. Each said what its own records supported at the time.
Both figures are on the same scale, which is exactly why they can be compared.

title: A notice somebody acts on
task: Put the four parts of the notice in the order they have to be read in.
scene: Adeyemi has two hundred words, and a town that has heard two different numbers and a rumour about a bigger one coming.
assumes: a public notice is read once, quickly, by somebody who is tired
takeaway: A notice earns its place by changing what somebody does, and everything else in it competes with that.
why: People act on the first thing they can use, so the instruction goes at the top. The reason comes next, because a reason is what makes an instruction survive being passed on. The revised number matters to scientists and changes nothing about what to do outside a building. The chance of aftershocks goes last, as a rate. As a rate it stays a chance. As a date it becomes a promise.

cards: What to do about the building you are standing outside.
That the number was revised from 6.6 to 6.8, and what that does and does not mean.
The chance of aftershocks, given as a rate for the week.

title: The slab is fine and the building is not
task: Say which explanation fits every observation.
scene: Navarro's survey: the slab is whole and level within itself, and the whole block has tipped. One side is down three hundred and forty millimetres, the other up ninety. Sand fans on the low side.
assumes: a foundation spreads a building's weight out into the ground
takeaway: A building can fail without anything in the building breaking.
question: Which explanation fits every observation?
why: Everything here points underneath the building rather than inside it. The slab is whole. The frame is straight. The whole block has tipped like a tray, one edge down and one edge up, with fresh sand pushed up on the low side. That is ground that stopped holding weight. Shake wet fill hard enough and the water takes the load, the grains stop pressing on each other, and one side sinks into it.
answerText: The ground gave way under one side and the building went with it. The whole slab and the straight frame are what say the fault is underneath.

choices: The frame failed, and the lean is damage inside the building.
The ground turned to liquid and stopped holding one side up.
The slab was built out of level, and this was here before the earthquake.
An aftershock hit the building from one side.
choiceMechanisms: A frame that gave way on one side would lean this way.
Ground that has gone liquid cannot hold the slab up, so the slab tips into it.
A mistake during building would leave a permanent lean.
One hard shove from one side could push a building over.
rebuttals: A frame that gave way shows it, and this one is straight to a tenth of a degree.
A mistake during building would have been visible for years, and it would not come with fresh sand on the ground.
One shove does not drop one edge by three hundred and forty millimetres and lift the other.
text.headline: A six-storey block stands eight degrees off upright, with nothing broken inside it.

title: What eight degrees does
task: Say what the lean actually costs.
scene: Okonkwo has the column loads out. At eight degrees the weight above each column no longer lands over the middle of it. The gap grows the higher you go.
assumes: a column is built to be pushed straight down, along its own length
takeaway: A column carrying its load off to one side is doing a job it was not built for.
question: What is the engineering objection to leaving Marina Court standing?
why: A column is strongest when the weight lands straight down its middle. Lean the building and that weight arrives off to one side, so the column is bent as well as squashed. Bending is the job it was not built for, and the offset grows the further up the building you go. The question is not how frightening eight degrees looks. It is whether those columns have enough left in them for a load path nobody designed.
answerText: The weight now lands off-centre, so the columns are bent as well as squashed. The frame is undamaged; the job it is being asked to do has changed.

choices: The lean will keep growing on its own until the building falls over.
The weight now lands off to one side, which bends columns built to be squashed.
A leaning building frightens people, and public confidence matters.
The frame was weakened by the tipping itself.
rebuttals: The lean stops when the water pressure underneath settles. It is not something that runs away by itself.
Frightened people are a real cost, and a reason to explain. They are not what makes a structure unsafe.
The frame is undamaged, which is exactly what the survey found.

title: What knocking it down would fix
task: Spend the five days of investigation on evidence that can change the town-wide decision.
scene: Halvorsen wants Marina Court pulled down this week. Delacroix has twelve blocks next to it on the same made ground, and five days before the fence is reviewed.
assumes: a decision can treat what you can see, or what caused it
takeaway: The best measurement is the one that could change a decision you have not made yet.
question: Which investigation buys something that helps beyond the one building already fenced off?
why: Pulling Marina Court down removes the building everybody can see. It says nothing about the ground under the twelve blocks on the same fill. Digging and testing that ground does. The fence already holds the hazard everybody knows about. So the five days are better spent on the question nobody has answered. More readings on one building answer a smaller question than the town is asking.
answerText: Buy the ground work along the corridor. The fence already holds Marina Court. Only the ground work says whether the twelve blocks beside it stand on the same problem.

title: A hall with nothing in the middle
task: Build the sideways load path, then name the link that decides whether it holds.
scene: The gym at Bay Road School has a long roof, heavy wall panels and nothing bracing it in the middle. One panel fixing tested badly. Everything big in there looks fine.
assumes: a sideways push has to travel through a building to reach the ground
takeaway: A load path works only if every link in it carries the force onward to the ground.
question: Which link decides whether the panel's push reaches the ground?
why: A shaking building throws its own weight sideways, and that push has to get to the ground. From the panel it goes into the fixing at the top. Then into the roof, along to a wall that can take it, and down. Every step has to hold. The panel is heavy and the roof is big, and neither matters if the small fixing between them lets go. Size is not strength when a link is missing.
answerText: Panel, fixing, roof, end wall, ground. The fixing at the top of the panel governs it. If that lets go, nothing bigger downstream can collect the panel's push.

title: What the tested fixings actually carried
task: Compare what the fixings carried with what the wall asks of them.
scene: Kirsten Sørensen has pulled two fixings out of a spare panel in the yard. The drawing says forty kilonewtons each. The first came out at twenty-four, the second at twenty-seven.
assumes: a number on a drawing is a claim, and a test is a check on it
takeaway: Two tests can show something is short. They cannot show a building is safe.
question: How does what the fixings carried compare with what is asked of them?
why: Two fixings were pulled. They averaged twenty-five and a half kilonewtons against thirty-one asked of them. So what was measured is about eight tenths of what is needed. That is short. It is also only two of them, and two is not enough to know how much the rest vary. None of that has to be settled before acting. Keep people out of the gym, test enough fixings to mean something, and design the repair.
answerText: About eight tenths of what the wall asks — short, and from only two tests.

estimate.prompt: The two fixings pulled out at twenty-four and twenty-seven kilonewtons. The wall asks about thirty-one kilonewtons of each of them.
estimate.question: How does what they carried compare with what is asked of them?
estimate.relationship: Compare = the average tested ÷ what is asked.
estimate.explanation: About eight tenths, which is under one. Two pulls do not settle the building. They settle whether this is worth acting on today.
estimate.solution: Twenty-four and twenty-seven average twenty-five and a half. That divided by thirty-one is about 0.8.
givens: The wall asks about 31 kilonewtons of each
labels: 31 kN (what the wall asks of each)

title: Four hundred children on Monday
task: Say what happens to the school on Monday.
scene: Four hundred children are due back Monday. The classrooms are sound and the gym is not. Halvorsen has parents calling, and there is no spare school to move anybody to.
assumes: a building can be used in part
takeaway: The question is which parts can be used, not whether the site is open or shut.
question: What should happen to Bay Road School on Monday?
why: The fault is in one room, so the decision belongs to rooms rather than to the site. The classrooms have nothing wrong with them. The gym has heavy panels held on by fixings that tested below what the wall asks. If children can reach the classrooms without passing under those panels, the classrooms open and the gym stays shut. If the routes cross, that gets fixed first. Part-open is not optimism. It is a fence round the actual fault.

choices: Open the whole site. The placard is green and the classrooms are undamaged.
Open the classrooms and shut the gym until the fixings are repaired.
Shut the whole site until every building on it has been looked at properly.
Open the site, and hold every class in the gym, which has no inside walls to fall.
rebuttals: The green placard covered what could be seen from outside, and the gym was locked that day.
Shutting the classrooms protects nobody. There is nothing wrong with them.
The gym is the worst room on the site, not the safest. Its walls hang on the fixings that tested short.

title: The part nobody has seen
task: Check what is behind each record, then spend the one visit before the placard review.
scene: Ninety patients are still on the ground floor, and two floors above them stand empty. The hospital has been yellow for three days. The roof plant room is locked, with two full water tanks in it.
assumes: a building's parts can be cleared one at a time
a signature says somebody approved it, not that somebody looked
takeaway: A signed record is worth whatever the looking behind it was worth.
question: Which claim still needs somebody to go and look?
why: A yellow placard should shrink to the specific things nobody has settled. The frame, the cladding and the stair have all been looked at, and there are notes to prove it. The roof plant room has not. Two full water tanks sit high in the building, and nobody has seen what holds them down. There is one visit left. Spending it on something already checked leaves the unchecked claim holding the review open.
answerText: Go to the roof plant room. The frame, cladding and stairs already have somebody's eyes behind them. The full tanks and their fixings are what nobody has seen, and that is what holds the review open.

title: What four more days buys
task: Put the cost of waiting into the same units as the risk.
scene: Tanaka has the aftershock rate for the week. Ives has the transfer log. Halvorsen wants both stated as what they cost, rather than as principles. The board meets on Friday.
assumes: waiting has consequences, and they can be counted
takeaway: Waiting is a decision, and it has to be compared with the decision to act now.
question: How should the office weigh four more days of evidence?
why: Both choices have a cost, and both can be counted. Waiting means transfers, delayed care and a hospital running short. Testing is worth it when it has a real chance of changing the answer. Here the frame has been looked at already, and the thing nobody has settled is a locked plant room with heavy tanks in it. Four days of coring answers a different question. Ask what the evidence could change, and who pays while it is collected.

choices: Evidence comes first. The delay is a shame, and it is not the engineer's problem.
Against what the waiting costs, and what the evidence could change.
By the aftershock forecast alone, since that is the hazard on the placard.
By what the hospital's managers want, since they carry the day-to-day risk.
rebuttals: Evidence first is a good instinct and not a rule. The question is what this evidence could change.
The forecast speaks to the hazard and says nothing about what an empty hospital costs.
Managers carry the day-to-day risk, and they do not get to set the engineering standard.

title: The instrument in the basement
task: Say what the basement record can and cannot settle.
scene: There is an instrument in the hospital basement, fitted in 1998 and never needed until now. Cardoso has its record. It peaked at 0.31 g. The building was designed for 0.35.
assumes: an instrument inside a building measures the shaking that building got
takeaway: Knowing what a building felt is worth a great deal, and it is not a line below which nothing breaks.
question: What can the basement record honestly add to the assessment?
why: The record takes the biggest unknown away. The ground under this building peaked at 0.31 g, and it was built for 0.35. That is worth a lot, and it is not a line under which nothing breaks. What a building feels also depends on which rhythms arrived and how long they lasted. So the record says the shaking was not obviously past the design. It says nothing about the tanks nobody has seen.

choices: That the building is undamaged, since the shaking stayed under the design figure.
That this building felt a little less than it was built for.
That the design figure was too low and should be raised.
That no more inspection is needed anywhere in the building.
rebuttals: Staying under a design figure makes damage less likely. It does not prove there is none.
One record from one earthquake is not grounds to change a design standard.
The plant room is still locked, so the inspection is not finished.

title: A number, with a method attached
task: Say what the four crushed cores actually support.
scene: Four cores, cut from the cracked columns. Sørensen crushes them: twenty-eight, thirty-one, twenty-four and thirty megapascals. The 1974 drawing asks for twenty-five.
assumes: concrete strength is measured by crushing a sample of it
takeaway: A test tells you about the concrete. It does not tell you about the column.
question: What is the strongest claim these four results support?
why: The four cores average close to what the drawing asked for, so weak concrete is not the story. That is worth knowing, and it is not the answer. Crushing a cylinder measures the material. It does not measure what the column went through, how much steel is inside it, or how well that steel wraps the concrete. The cores narrow the question. Somebody still has to work out what the column can carry now.

choices: That the columns are undamaged, since the concrete beats what was specified.
That the concrete is as strong as the design assumed, which is one input and not the answer.
That the design was too careful, and the building is stronger than it needs to be.
That the cracking must have come from something other than the earthquake.
rebuttals: Cracking is something you see in the structure. A crushed core says nothing about it either way.
One building's concrete beating its specification says nothing about whether the design was careful.
Cracks running diagonally in a ground-floor column during an earthquake have an obvious cause.

title: Which way the cracks run
task: Say which explanation fits the pattern.
scene: The cracks run diagonally, both ways, crossing in an X across the middle of each column. They are fine, there are many, and they sit evenly apart.
assumes: a crack opens across the direction something is being pulled apart
takeaway: A pattern can point at the cause. It cannot tell you what is left.
question: Which explanation fits the pattern?
why: Concrete cracks across whatever is pulling it apart. Push a column sideways and the pull runs on a diagonal, so the crack opens on a diagonal. Push it back and a second diagonal opens, crossing the first. That X is the mark of shaking, not of weight or of slow settling. Many fine cracks rather than one big one also says the steel inside is working. It does not say how much is left.

choices: Being pushed side to side, first one way and then the other.
Too much weight pressing straight down.
The foundation settling slowly over years.
Poor concrete.
choiceMechanisms: A push one way and then back opens cracks running both ways.
Too much weight crushes concrete and bursts the outer layer off.
Settling bends a frame slowly, and in one direction.
Weak material cracks under everyday loads.
rebuttals: Crushing pushes the outer layer of concrete off, and the cover here is untouched.
Settling works slowly and one way. It does not open crossed diagonals.
The cores came back above what was specified, so weak material is not it.
text.headline: Fine diagonal cracks cross both ways across three ground-floor columns.

title: Part of a building, for part of a purpose
task: Put the four steps in the order they have to happen.
scene: Monday's public meeting has two hundred people booked. There is no other hall big enough. Three ground-floor columns in the library are cracked.
assumes: use can be limited by how many people, by which rooms, and for how long
takeaway: Restricted use is a real answer between open and shut, and it has to say what it is protecting against.
why: Part-use is an engineering line, not a hopeful label. Propping comes first, because it changes what the building can carry. A number on the door comes next. A limit nobody can count is not a limit. A review date comes after that, or the restriction quietly turns permanent and stops being believed. Only then is the meeting a yes or a no.

cards: Prop the three cracked columns, to take weight off them.
Set a limit on how many people, and put it on the door.
Put a review date on the limit, so it ends rather than drifts.
Decide whether Monday's meeting can be held in the building.

title: Three reasons wearing one line
task: Check what is behind each stretch of fence, then spend the one field check.
scene: Shopkeepers wait at the tape with keys in their hands. Delacroix walks the line with the log. Three stretches have written reasons. The southern leg has none that anybody can point to.
assumes: a fence can be up for more than one reason
checking costs time, and there is one check left before the map is reissued
takeaway: Every stretch of fence is a claim about a hazard, and a claim should be checkable.
question: Which closure most needs somebody to go and check the ground?
why: A cordon usually holds several different hazards, and each one has its own condition for coming down. The Parade is closed for the masonry overhead. The gas leg waits on the utility. Ferry Street is about heavy vehicles getting through. The southern leg is different. The map keeps people out and the log gives no reason. One check is left, and the unbacked line is the one to spend it on.
answerText: Check the southern leg. Every other stretch has a written hazard behind it. If there is a hazard there, record it and keep the fence. If there is not, the line should not stay up because somebody drew it on the first night.

title: Soft ground, three days on
task: Say what state Ferry Street is really in.
scene: Thandi Mbeki has been out on Ferry Street with a hand auger. The sand has dried and the water has dropped back. The surface carries a person, and not a truck.
assumes: ground that went liquid gets its strength back as the water pressure drops
takeaway: The liquid part is over quickly. What it leaves behind is not.
question: What is the honest status of Ferry Street now?
why: Ground goes liquid while the water in it is under pressure, and that pressure drains away within hours. So the liquid part is finished. The ground it left is not the ground that was there before. It has settled unevenly, spread sideways, and lost sand up through the surface, which leaves holes underneath. Dry on top says nothing about whether a truck is safe. And the same layer can go again in a big aftershock.

choices: Still liquid, and dangerous to anybody walking on it.
Drained and disturbed. Walkable, no heavy vehicles, and liable to go again.
Fully recovered, since the water has gone and the surface is dry.
Ruined for good, and the street will have to be rebuilt before anybody returns.
rebuttals: The water pressure drains away in hours, so it is not still liquid three days later.
Dry on top is not recovered underneath. The ground has been rearranged.
Nothing here says the street is beyond repair, and most ground like this is repaired rather than replaced.

title: A condition, not a date
task: Say what the office should promise.
scene: Halvorsen wants a date. Delacroix wants a condition. Tanaka says a date is a promise about the ground, and a condition is a promise about the office.
assumes: a promise can be tied to a day, or to something anybody can check
takeaway: Tie a decision to something somebody can check, and it stays honest whatever the ground does next.
question: What should the office commit to?
why: A date promises how the ground will behave, and nobody controls that. A condition promises what the office will require before it moves a fence, and the office does control that. Publishing the conditions turns waiting into something people can watch. The aftershock rate is a poor trigger, because it says nothing about one street. Name the checks that open each stretch.

choices: A date. The fence comes down on Friday.
A condition. Each stretch opens when the hazard written against it is fixed.
A rate. The fence comes down when aftershocks drop below one a day.
No promise at all, until every building inside the fence has been fully assessed.
rebuttals: A date promises how the ground and the repairs will behave, and nobody can promise that.
The aftershock rate is not the hazard written against any of these stretches.
Fully assessing every building would take a month, and most of these streets do not need it.

title: Measuring against the wrong zero
task: Open what each conclusion rests on, keep the ones that stand alone, and name what the rest share.
scene: Cardoso's five-day check is finished. The station everything was compared against shakes more than it should. Navarro lays five of the fortnight's conclusions beside it.
assumes: a comparison is only as good as the thing you compared against
takeaway: A bad reference spoils whatever leaned on it, and leaves what was measured directly alone.
question: Which conclusions inherit the bad reference, and which stand on their own?
why: Every conclusion has a chain under it, and the question is whether the vault sits in that chain. The Flats figure was measured against the vault, so it moves. The vault itself shakes about 1.6 times what solid rock does, so three times the vault is nearer five times rock. Anything copied from that figure moves too. The hospital's own record and the Marina Court survey never touched it.
answerText: Redo the Flats figure and anything copied from it. Three times a vault that is itself 1.6 times rock is about five times rock. Keep the hospital's 0.31 g, the magnitude and the Marina Court diagnosis — none of them used the vault.

title: What still stands
task: Sort the fortnight's conclusions by what they rest on.
scene: Navarro puts four of the fortnight's conclusions on the board and asks which of them leaned on the vault. The corrected vault report is clipped up beside them.
assumes: a conclusion can rest on one measurement or on several
takeaway: A bad reference spoils what was measured against it, and leaves what was measured directly.
why: Follow each conclusion down to what it rests on. The Flats figure used the vault as its yardstick, so a bad yardstick moves it. Marina Court was worked out from a survey, from heave and from sand. The hospital's number came from its own basement. The parapet case rests on what people watched fall. Those three may deserve other checks, and this error is not one of them.

scenarios: The Flats shake about three times as hard.
Marina Court failed because the ground stopped holding it up.
The hospital saw 0.31 g against a design of 0.35.
The Parade's parapets need tying back.
choices: Falls, and has to be restated. The real figure is nearer five.
Stands. Survey, heave and sand, with no station in it.
Stands. Measured by the hospital's own instrument.
Stands. Something people watched, rather than a comparison.
rebuttals: That factor was the vault comparison, so it is the one conclusion that falls.
Marina Court was worked out from settlement, heave and sand, with no station involved.
The hospital's shaking was measured in its own basement.
The parapet case rests on every parapet having come down, which is something people saw.
columns: What the vault error does to it

title: Five times, not three
task: Say what the corrected figure changes.
scene: If the Flats shake five times as hard as rock rather than three, a future earthquake delivers far more there. The district map is waiting on a new number.
assumes: design figures come from the shaking that is expected
takeaway: Fixing what you expect changes what gets built next. It does not change what already happened.
question: What does the corrected figure change?
why: The placards came from people looking at buildings, so a corrected figure does not move them. What it moves is everything still to be decided. Rebuilding in the Flats is designed against expected shaking, and that expectation just went up. So has the case for improving the ground first. One number is not a whole design either. It changes the future, not the past.

choices: The placards issued this fortnight, which used the wrong figure.
The figures for rebuilding in the Flats, and the case for improving that ground.
The size of the earthquake that has already happened.
Nothing, because the buildings have already been through the real shaking.
rebuttals: Placards came from looking at damage, not from a predicted figure.
The magnitude belongs to the earthquake, and it is worked out from many stations.
Buildings that survived did so under this shaking, which says nothing about the next one.

title: Which of the three cannot wait
task: Keep the one judgement nobody else can make, and hand the rest over properly.
scene: Three calls land within minutes. A burst main is pouring water into the Flats. Buildings need checking after the 5.1. The school reopening message has to go out. Four engineers are free.
assumes: a problem still getting worse is different from one that has finished
takeaway: Keep the judgement nobody else can make, and hand the rest over with a first move and a number.
question: How do you split the team across the three?
why: The burst main is still making the ground worse. So it gets stopped first, and stopping it belongs to the utility rather than to you. The 5.1 is over, and nobody knows what it did to the propped buildings. That is the judgement nobody else here can make, so you keep it. The school decision is settled and only needs saying. Three at once is not a queue. It is a split.
answerText: Keep the checks on the propped buildings yourself. Send the utility liaison to shut the main now. Give the school message to the desk. Every handover gets an owner, a first move and a number.

title: Wetting ground that has already failed
task: Say why the burst main matters more here than uphill.
scene: Mbeki is on Ferry Street with a standpipe. The water under the road has risen three quarters of a metre since the main went. The surface is soft underfoot again.
assumes: ground can only go liquid if it is full of water
takeaway: Wetting loose ground uses up the margin it had before the next shake.
question: Why does the burst main matter more here than it would in Upper Town?
why: Ground holds things up because the grains press on each other. Water in the gaps carries some of the load instead. The more water there is, the less the grains carry. Loose wet fill is already near the edge, and a burst main pushes it closer before any shaking starts. The leak alone will not make it go liquid. It means a smaller shake will.

choices: Because the Flats have older pipes, and more of them will burst.
Because more water in loose fill lifts the water pressure before any shaking starts.
Because the water washes away the sand that came up in the first event.
Because the fill will dissolve if it stays wet long enough.
rebuttals: Pipe age explains why it burst, and not why it matters more on this ground.
Moving sand about is a nuisance. The water pressure is the part that matters.
Sand does not dissolve, and the fill is not going anywhere. Its strength is the problem.

title: A smaller shake against a weaker building
task: Say what the new cracks tell the office.
scene: The 5.1 shook the Flats about a tenth as hard as the first earthquake. Eleven buildings have been propped since Friday, and two of them have new cracks this afternoon.
assumes: a propped building is being held up, not repaired
takeaway: A small shake that still does damage is telling you how little the building has left.
question: What do the two buildings with new cracks tell the office?
why: Props hold a building up. They do not put back what the earthquake took out of it. So a shake a tenth the size doing fresh damage says something specific. Those two are working near the limit of what they have left. That is a reason to tighten the restrictions and look again before anybody talks about repairs. It is not proof that the props failed, and it does not say how close to falling either building is.

choices: That the props failed, and should be swapped for something else.
That those two are near the limit of what they have left, which is what the props bought time against.
That the aftershock was much bigger in those two streets than the network says.
That the first assessment of both buildings was wrong.
rebuttals: The props are still standing and doing their job. Nothing about them failed.
Stations either side of those streets recorded the same shaking, so it was not worse there.
The first assessment said those buildings had little left, which is exactly what this confirms.

title: Measured, worked out, or guessed
task: Sort the four findings by the evidence under them.
scene: Cardoso lays out four statements from the fortnight. The office believes all four. They are not believed for the same reasons, and she will not let them into the report as equals.
assumes: a claim can rest on a measurement, on reasoning, or on nothing much yet
takeaway: Sorting findings by their evidence is what lets the next reader know which one to check first.
why: These four are believed for four different reasons, and the report should say which. The vault error was dug up, logged, and checked against another station for five days. The hospital's number came from its own basement, once. Marina Court's cause is good reasoning from a survey, with nobody having dug under the slab. The last one is a guess about the future. Saying so does not weaken the report.

scenarios: The reference vault sits on weathered granite, not solid rock.
The hospital felt 0.31 g at its base.
Marina Court tipped because the ground stopped holding it up.
The Flats will shake about five times as hard in a future earthquake.
choices: Settled. A 1998 trench log, and five days of side-by-side records.
Measured once, at one building, for one earthquake.
Worked out. Good ground reasoning from a survey, with no hole dug under the slab.
A projection. The weakest claim in the report, and the one the plan leans on.
rebuttals: The vault error has a trench log and five days of side-by-side recording behind it.
The hospital's number came from an instrument in its own basement, for one earthquake.
Marina Court's cause is sound reasoning from a survey, with no hole dug under the slab.
How the fill behaves next time is a projection, and it is the weakest claim here.

title: The number that has to be a range
task: Say why the forecast goes in as a range.
scene: Tanaka's aftershock forecast goes into the report. She wants the range in the sentence. Okonkwo wants to know what the range is for. The staffing appendix waits on the wording.
assumes: a forecast covers a spread of outcomes, not just one
takeaway: A forecast with no range cannot size a decision, because the decision is sized against the range.
question: Why does the forecast go in as a range rather than one number?
why: Nobody staffs an emergency for an average week. They staff it for a bad one, and how bad is exactly what the range says. Give a planner one number and they invent a margin themselves, usually too small. The range is also the honest half of the forecast. It says which part of the behaviour four hundred recorded aftershocks pin down well, and which part they do not. One number hides both.

choices: Because a range is more careful, and careful is right after something like this.
Because people plan against the bad end, and one number deletes it.
Because the model is not good enough yet to give one number honestly.
Because a range cannot be shown to be wrong afterwards.
rebuttals: Care is not the reason. The range is a number the staffing sum actually needs.
How good the model is, is what the range states. That is the opposite of hiding it.
A range can be shown to be wrong. Outcomes outside it count against the model.

title: What outlives the emergency
task: Choose the practice worth keeping when nothing is happening.
scene: Four things the office started doing under pressure. Okonkwo asks which is worth its cost on an ordinary Tuesday, when nothing has happened.
assumes: a habit taken up in an emergency has a cost that only shows later
takeaway: An unknown gets safer only when it has an owner, a date, and a rule that stops it being forgotten.
question: Which practice would most directly stop this happening again?
why: A habit worth keeping catches the mistakes that keep happening, at a price the office will still pay in a quiet year. The gym, the plant room and the Ferry Street basement were all outside what anybody looked at. In every case somebody knew. Writing that list down, and giving it an owner, would have caught all three. A rule nobody keeps is worse than no rule.

choices: Write down, on every inspection, the parts of the building nobody could see.
Two engineers on every placard, which halves how many buildings get cleared.
A daily public meeting, which took two hours out of every afternoon.
Re-inspect every propped building after any aftershock above magnitude 4.
rebuttals: Doubling up halves how many buildings get cleared in a day, for a mistake rate nobody has measured.
A daily meeting was right during the emergency, and no office keeps that up for years.
A rule that fires on every magnitude 4 gets dropped in the first quiet year, which is worse than no rule.
